Checking the identification assumptions

Source: vignettes/rddid-validation-tests.Rmd
rddid-validation-tests.Rmd

Get started runs the four tests and reads their printouts. This article adds how each statistic is built, the tests under the ATU design, their options, and how the four results read together.

When the tests apply

The tests are for a panel in which the running variable moves over time, so that some units, the switchers, are above the cutoff in one period and below it in another. The units at the cutoff in the RD period can then be a different mix from the units at the cutoff in a comparison period, and the difference of the two jumps can mix the treatment effect with that difference in who is at the cutoff. A unit’s type records its side of the cutoff in other periods; the table in Get started gives the two versions the tests use. The RD-DID estimate identifies the ATT when

  1. type continuity holds,
  2. constant within-type confounding holds, and
  3. composition stability or homogeneous confounding holds (one of the two is enough).

This is the paper’s result for a time-varying running variable (Leventer and Nevo, 2024). There is one test per assumption. When the running variable does not move, as in rddid_sim, every unit has the same type in every period and the tests are not informative; in a repeated cross-section the types are not observed.

The examples use rddid_sim_pv: the rddid_sim design (a confounding jump of 0.5 in every year, a treatment effect of 1 in year 3, the RD period) with a running variable that drifts between years. Most units stay on one side; some switch:

library(rddid)
above <- rddid_sim_pv$R >= 0
switcher <- tapply(above, rddid_sim_pv$id, function(a) length(unique(a)) > 1)
sum(switcher)
#> [1] 176

Every test takes the same long data frame and column names as rddid(). By default each test uses the bias-corrected jumps with their robust variances (bc = TRUE), like the Robust (bias-corrected) row of rddid(). The two tests on type shares pick a separate CCT bandwidth for every local-linear fit (bwselect = "cct") and combine their jumps with a studentized sup-t statistic (joint = "supt", studentize = TRUE); the two tests on the outcome use one bandwidth for every cell (bwselect = "pooled"). The last section says why.

Type continuity: rd_typecont()

H0: the share of each type jumps by zero at the cutoff, in every period.

tc <- rd_typecont(rddid_sim_pv, x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3)
tc
#> Test of type continuity  [rd_typecont()]
#>   H0: the share of each type jumps by zero at the cutoff, in every period
#>   Sampling scheme: panel, some units change side of the cutoff (detected)
#>   Periods: 1, 2, 3   Types: ++, +-, -+, --   Bandwidth: CCT MSE-optimal, chosen per cell
#>   Type in a period: a unit's sides of the cutoff in the other periods, in time order
#>     ("+" at or above, "-" below).
#> 
#>   Joint sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 1.232 over 9 jumps,  p = 0.869  (largest: period:type 1:+-)
#>     Period 1: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 1.232 over 3 jumps,  p = 0.500
#>     Period 2: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 0.582 over 3 jumps,  p = 0.902
#>     Period 3: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 1.048 over 3 jumps,  p = 0.633
#>   All joint statistics: x$joint_tests
  • Types: ++, +-, -+, --: a unit’s sides of the cutoff in the other two years, in time order (the first row of the type table in Get started).
  • The test runs, in each year and for each type, a local-linear RD of the indicator “the unit is of this type” on the running variable; the jump is the difference between the type’s share just above and just below the cutoff.
  • Joint sup-t (studentized) ... over 9 jumps: in each year the four shares sum to one, so three jumps are free; three years give 9. Each jump is divided by its standard error, and the largest |t| is compared with the sup-t critical value: the quantile of the largest |t| when every share is continuous, from the estimated correlation of the nine jumps and, since each standard error is itself an estimate, with t rather than normal tails. The printout names the year and type with the largest |t|. The Period lines test each year alone.

Here p = 0.869. Type continuity holds in rddid_sim_pv by construction, so a p-value below 0.05 would be a false rejection.

If it rejects: units sort around the cutoff according to their side in other periods, so the jump in the outcome partly reflects a jump in who the units are. The RD-DID estimate can then be biased, whatever the other tests say.

Composition stability: rd_compstable()

H0: the share of each type among the units just above the cutoff is the same in the RD period and in each comparison period.

cs <- rd_compstable(rddid_sim_pv, x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3)
cs
#> Test of composition stability  [rd_compstable()]
#>   H0: the share of each type among the units just above the cutoff is the same in the RD period and in each comparison period
#>   Sampling scheme: panel, some units change side of the cutoff (detected)
#>   RD period: 3   Comparison periods: 1, 2   Bandwidth: CCT MSE-optimal, chosen per cell
#> 
#>   Pair 3::1: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 3.086 over 3 jumps,  p = 0.009
#>     n above the cutoff: 490 (RD period), 508 (comparison), 430 in both
#>   Pair 3::2: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 2.059 over 3 jumps,  p = 0.120
#>     n above the cutoff: 490 (RD period), 497 (comparison), 418 in both
#> 
#>   Joint over pairs: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 3.086 over 6 jumps,  p = 0.016  (largest: pair:type 3::1:-+)
#>   All joint statistics: x$joint_tests
  • One block per pair of the RD period and a comparison period: Pair 3::1 compares year 3 with year 1. The types are those of type continuity (a unit’s sides in the other two years), so there are four types and three free shares (over 3 jumps).
  • The test stacks the units above the cutoff in the two years, with the comparison year’s running variable reflected below an artificial cutoff, and tests the jump in each type share there.
  • n above the cutoff: the units above the cutoff in the RD year, in the comparison year, and in both. Units above the cutoff in both years appear on both sides of the stacked regression; the standard error accounts for them.
  • Joint over pairs: one sup-t test over the jumps of both pairs (six here), with their full covariance. The pairs share the RD-period units, and in a panel also the units above the cutoff in both comparison years, so their jumps are correlated; the covariance across pairs comes from those shared units.

Here p = 0.016. Composition stability is false in rddid_sim_pv by construction: the units at the year-3 cutoff were mostly on the same side in years 1 and 2, while the units at the year-1 cutoff are spread evenly over the four types. A rejection here is a correct detection; with 1,000 units the test does not always detect it.

If it rejects: the units at the cutoff in the RD period are a different mix of types from those in a comparison period. If the confounding jump also differs across types, the comparison-period jump measures the confounding jump of a different mix, and the estimate can be biased. If the confounding jump is the same for every type (the next test), the mix does not matter and the estimate is still valid.

Homogeneous confounding: rd_homog()

H0: in each comparison period the confounding jump is the same for every type.

Here a unit’s type is its side of the cutoff in the RD period (the second row of the type table in Get started; type_by = "rd_side", the default).

hg <- rd_homog(rddid_sim_pv, y = "Y", x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3)
hg
#> Test of homogeneous confounding  [rd_homog()]
#>   H0: in each comparison period the confounding jump is the same for every type
#>   Sampling scheme: panel, some units change side of the cutoff (detected)
#>   Comparison periods: 1, 2   Bandwidth: h = 0.2104 in every cell (CCT on the pooled comparison periods)
#> 
#>   Type: a unit's side of the cutoff in RD period 3 ("+" at or above, "-" below).
#>   Wald chi-squared(2) = 0.247,  p = 0.884
#> 
#>   Per-cell local-linear jumps (comparison periods):
#>     Period     Type               jump       s.e.       n
#>     1          -                0.5347     0.2640     510  (reference)
#>     1          +                0.7070     0.4047     490
#>     2          -                1.0987     0.4183     510  (reference)
#>     2          +                0.8699     0.5244     490
  • The table gives, in each comparison year, the jump in the outcome at the cutoff among the units below (-) and above (+) the cutoff in year 3. In a comparison period the jump is the confounding jump, so these are the confounding jumps by type.
  • Wald chi-squared(2): one contrast (type + against the reference type -) per comparison year.
  • Bandwidth: one bandwidth in every cell, the CCT bandwidth of the outcome with both comparison years pooled.

Here p = 0.884. The null is true in rddid_sim_pv (the confounding jump is 0.5 for every unit), so a p-value below 0.05 would be a false rejection. The per-type jumps are imprecise (standard errors 0.26 to 0.52).

If it rejects: the confounding jump differs across types. If composition stability holds, a confounding jump that differs across types does not bias the estimate. If both nulls are false, the estimate can be biased.

Constant within-type confounding: rd_trendcell()

H0: within each type, the confounding jump is the same in every comparison period.

tr <- rd_trendcell(rddid_sim_pv, y = "Y", x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3)
tr
#> Test of constant within-type confounding  [rd_trendcell()]
#>   H0: within each type, the confounding jump is the same in every comparison period
#>   Sampling scheme: panel, some units change side of the cutoff (detected)
#>   Comparison periods: 1, 2   Trend: constant
#>   Bandwidth: h = 0.2104 in every cell (CCT on the pooled comparison periods)
#> 
#>   Type: a unit's side of the cutoff in RD period 3 ("+" at or above, "-" below).
#>   Wald chi-squared(2) = 1.445,  p = 0.485
#> 
#>   Per-cell local-linear jumps (comparison periods):
#>     Type       Period             jump       s.e.       n
#>     +          1                0.7070     0.4047     490  (reference)
#>     +          2                0.8699     0.5244     490
#>     -          1                0.5347     0.2640     510  (reference)
#>     -          2                1.0987     0.4183     510
  • The per-cell jumps are those of rd_homog(), compared the other way: rd_homog() compares types within a comparison period, rd_trendcell() compares comparison periods within a type.
  • Wald chi-squared(2): one contrast (year 2 against year 1) per type.

This is a pre-trends check. The assumption concerns the RD period, where the confounding jump cannot be separated from the effect, so the test asks whether the within-type confounding jump is stable across the comparison periods. Not rejecting does not establish the assumption in the RD period. Here p = 0.485.

With trend = "linear" the null is that the within-type confounding jump moves linearly across the comparison periods. That needs at least three comparison periods; with two, the function says so and returns no statistic.

If it rejects: the within-type confounding jump changes over time, and constant weights do not cancel it. rddid(trend = "linear") allows a within-type confounding jump that moves linearly in time, and rd_trendcell(trend = "linear") tests that version (three or more comparison periods).

ATU designs

When everybody is treated in the comparison periods (estimand = "atu"), the estimate concerns the units just below the cutoff, and composition stability concerns the below-cutoff shares. rd_compstable(estimand = "atu") mirrors the running variable and runs the same test on the units below the cutoff; the other three tests give the same numbers with either estimand, so estimand only labels them. rddid_sim_pv is an ATT design, so the call below only shows the mechanics:

rd_compstable(rddid_sim_pv, x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3, estimand = "atu")
#> Test of composition stability  [rd_compstable()]
#>   H0: the share of each type among the units just below the cutoff is the same in the RD period and in each comparison period
#>   Sampling scheme: panel, some units change side of the cutoff (detected)
#>   Estimand: ATU (the units below the cutoff are the ones untreated in the RD period, so the test is on their shares (mirrored design))
#>   RD period: 3   Comparison periods: 1, 2   Bandwidth: CCT MSE-optimal, chosen per cell
#> 
#>   Pair 3::1: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 1.901 over 3 jumps,  p = 0.166
#>     n below the cutoff: 510 (RD period), 492 (comparison), 432 in both
#>   Pair 3::2: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 1.705 over 3 jumps,  p = 0.240
#>     n below the cutoff: 510 (RD period), 503 (comparison), 431 in both
#> 
#>   Joint over pairs: sup-t (t critical values) max |t| = 1.901 over 6 jumps,  p = 0.293  (largest: pair:type 3::1:++)
#>   All joint statistics: x$joint_tests

In this printout the H0 line and the counts refer to the units below the cutoff: under the ATU design those are the units untreated in the RD period, whose composition the estimate relies on.

Run all four at once: rd_checks() 

ch <- rd_checks(rddid_sim_pv, y = "Y", x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3)
ch
#> Tests of the identification assumptions  [rd_checks()]
#> 
#>   Assumption                          Statistic        p   Statistic type             Bandwidth
#>   type continuity                         1.232    0.869   sup-t, t critical values   CCT per cell
#>   composition stability                   3.086    0.016   sup-t, t critical values   CCT per cell
#>   homogeneous confounding                 0.247    0.884   Wald chi-squared(2)        pooled CCT, h = 0.21
#>   constant within-type confounding        1.445    0.485   Wald chi-squared(2)        pooled CCT, h = 0.21
#> 
#>   Reading at level 0.95, rejecting when p < 0.05 (not rejecting does not establish an assumption):
#>     type continuity                    not rejected
#>     composition stability              rejected     } identification needs
#>     homogeneous confounding            not rejected } only one of these two
#>     constant within-type confounding   not rejected (checked in the comparison periods)
#>   Each test's details: x$typecont, x$compstable, x$homog, x$trendcell.

rd_checks() runs the four tests with one set of options and prints one row per test, with the statistic, its type and the bandwidth rule. The four results are inside (ch$typecont, …), and tidy(ch) returns the table for a paper or a table maker such as modelsummary. The statistic column holds the largest |t| for the two share tests (sup-t) and the chi-squared statistic for the two outcome tests.

Together, the four results map onto the list at the top. A rejection of type continuity, or of constant within-type confounding, would call the estimate into question; so would a rejection of both composition stability and homogeneous confounding. A rejection of only one of those two would not on its own, because either one is enough for identification. In rddid_sim_pv the truth is known: composition stability fails and the other three assumptions hold, so the estimate is valid:

rddid(rddid_sim_pv, y = "Y", x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3)
#> RD-DID estimate of the ATT in period 3
#>   Comparison periods: 1, 2   (constant confounding trend)
#>   Comparison weights: 1: 0.500, 2: 0.500
#>   Sampling scheme: panel, some units change side of the cutoff (detected)
#>   Bandwidth: common h = 0.2367 (rule "joint": one bandwidth, chosen for the RD-DID estimate)
#>   Pilot bandwidth b (period = value): 1 = 0.3889, 2 = 0.3847, 3 = 0.3933
#> 
#>                              Estimate  Std. err.       z  p-value   95% CI
#>   Conventional                 0.9654     0.1933    4.99   <0.001   [0.5866, 1.3442]
#>   Robust (bias-corrected)      0.9823     0.2292    4.29   <0.001   [0.5332, 1.4315]
#> 
#>   summary() shows the per-period fits and the s.e. under every sampling scheme.

The true effect is 1.

Why sup-t, and a pooled bandwidth for the outcome tests

In simulations with a clean null (every assumption true, 1,000 units, three periods, 5% level), the chi-squared Wald statistics with per-cell bandwidths rejected a true null too often: 9% for the share tests and 8% for the outcome tests. The excess comes from the estimated covariance of the jumps, not from the jumps themselves, in two ways.

  • A bandwidth chosen on each cell’s own data is noisy, and the variance formula treats it as fixed, so each variance comes out 10-15% too small. For the outcome tests, whose cells are thin, one bandwidth chosen on the pooled comparison periods removes this: 6% instead of 8%, at about 8 points of power against a violation confined to one cell.
  • A chi-squared Wald inverts a 6-by-6 or 9-by-9 covariance estimated from a few hundred units near the cutoff, and the error in that inverse grows with the number of jumps (15% at 28 jumps, four periods). sup-t and sWald use the covariance only through its correlations, so they avoid that inversion: 6-7% at three periods, 4-5% at four. They still divide each jump by its estimated standard error, so a variance that is too small, or noisy, inflates them as well, by less than the Wald; that is why the share tests stay slightly above 5% at three periods. For the share tests the per-fit bandwidth is kept, because it adapts to a sorting window and every pooled bandwidth tried halved the power against local sorting.

The default sup-t is studentized: each standard error is an estimate, with the degrees of freedom of its robust variance (about 50-150 here, computed from each jump’s regression weights), and the critical value accounts for that noise. With the same simulations the studentized sup-t rejected a true null about 6% of the time at three periods and 4-5% at four, against 7% and 5-6% for sup-t with normal critical values, with the same power once the sizes are matched.

With two periods (one jump per test and period) the statistics are the same two-sided test, and the share tests did not over-reject.

Switching options

The defaults are the settings recommended above; every alternative is one argument away, in each test and in rd_checks().

# share tests: the chi-squared Wald, or sup-t with normal critical values
rd_typecont(rddid_sim_pv, x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3, joint = "wald")
rd_typecont(rddid_sim_pv, x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3, studentize = FALSE)
# outcome tests: one bandwidth per cell instead of one pooled bandwidth
rd_homog(rddid_sim_pv, y = "Y", x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3, bwselect = "cct")
# all four at once, and one test differently from the others
rd_checks(rddid_sim_pv, y = "Y", x = "R", time = "year", id = "id", t_rd = 3,
          joint = "wald", outcome_bwselect = "cct", homog = list(min_n = 20))

Every statistic of a share test is also in $joint_tests, so the alternatives can be compared without running the test again:

ch$typecont$joint_tests
#>   method   reference statistic df   p_value
#> 1   supt           t  1.231775  9 0.8693313
#> 2   supt      normal  1.231775  9 0.8621414
#> 3  swald           t  5.110313  9 0.7955420
#> 4  swald      normal  5.110313  9 0.7861821
#> 5   wald chi-squared  4.781633  9 0.8529133

Options

  • bwselect: for rd_typecont() and rd_compstable(), "cct" (default) chooses a CCT bandwidth for every local-linear fit and "rot" uses a rule of thumb; for rd_homog() and rd_trendcell(), "pooled" (default) uses the CCT bandwidth of the outcome on the pooled comparison periods in every cell, "cct" one per cell, "rot" a rule of thumb. h fixes the bandwidth.
  • joint (rd_typecont(), rd_compstable()): "supt" (default), "swald" (the sum of squared t’s) or "wald" (the chi-squared Wald); studentize: TRUE (default, t-based critical values for sup-t and sWald) or FALSE (normal). Every combination is in $joint_tests.
  • bc: TRUE (default) tests the bias-corrected jumps with their robust variances; FALSE uses the conventional ones.
  • scheme: detected from the data as in rddid(); set it to override.
  • rd_homog(): type_by = "rd_side" (default, the side in the RD period) or "pattern" (the sides in the other periods used). rd_trendcell() always types units by their side in the RD period.
  • rd_homog() and rd_trendcell(): min_n drops cells with too few observations on either side of the cutoff, with a message.

The article How rddid() computes the estimate rebuilds the type-continuity and composition-stability tests by hand and runs all four on simulated designs in which one assumption fails at a time, with the resulting bias in the estimate.

Reference

Leventer, D. and D. Nevo (2024). Correcting Invalid Regression Discontinuity Designs Using Multiple Time-Period Data. arXiv:2408.05847. https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05847
